subject: history
title: Workers, Towns & Reform Adventure
welcome_lead: Life in Victorian factory towns was tough — long hours, child labour and dirty streets. But reformers were fighting back. 🏭
meta_desc: Workers & Reform Adventure — a KS3 walkthrough of working conditions, child labour and Victorian reforms.
final_note: You met the harsh world of Victorian workers and the reforms — like the 1833 Factory Act — that slowly improved life.

concepts.def: Work done by children, often very young
Deadly disease spread by dirty water
Group of workers asking for better conditions

walkthroughs.body_html:
Cities like Manchester and Leeds grew massively, but conditions were poor.

Workers' families crammed into tiny back-to-back houses in slums. There were no proper toilets and water often came from polluted wells.

Diseases like cholera killed thousands. Smoke from coal fires turned the air thick and grey. 🌫️

Factories used many children because they were small, cheap and could climb under machines.

Children as young as 5 or 6 worked in cotton mills and coal mines. Days could be 12–14 hours. Accidents were common.

Writers like Charles Dickens showed how harsh life was for poor children, in books like Oliver Twist.

Reformers slowly forced changes through Parliament:

  • 1833 Factory Act — no children under 9 in textile factories; under-13s limited to 9 hours.
  • 1842 Mines Act — no women or boys under 10 underground.
  • 1870 Education Act — schools for all children.

Workers also formed trade unions to push for fairer pay and shorter hours. By 1900 life in Britain was still hard, but better than in 1800.
